messages.body_plain:
Dear Bryan,

Thank you very much!
 I managed to get around this, basically by converting data into matrix, then an array and keeping dimensions in check

Lisso.means<-lapply(coords.subset(gdf$shape, classifier$Species), FUN = mshape)
Lisso.means1<-as.matrix(Lisso.means)

Lisso.means2<-arrayspecs(Lisso.means1, 13, 3)
dimnames(Lisso.means2)

identical (dimnames (Lisso.means2)[[3]], LissoPhy$tip.label)
newOrder <- match (LissoPhy$tip.label, dimnames (Lisso.means2)[[3]])

Lisso.means3<-Lisso.means2[,,newOrder, drop=FALSE]

identical (dimnames (Lisso.means3)[[3]], LissoPhy$tip.label)

And now I finally get TRUE for "identical" function.

However, when I try to do a simple phylo analysis

Lissosignal<-physignal(Lisso.means4, phy=LissoPhy, iter = 999, seed = NULL, print.progress = FALSE)

I still get an error:

Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)) :

  error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function 'tcrossprod': non-numeric argument to mathematical function

I'm probably still making some data formatting errors because the algorithm won't recognize my shape data as numeric.

All the best,
Aleksandar

Lisso.means <- lapply(coords.subset(ScapA, classifier$Species), FUN = mshape)

[1] "array"

[1] "phylo"

All the best,

messages.body_plain:
OK, you did not indicate which version of geomorph you are using but I am not sure it matters, as the version of RRPP and the version of R are quite old.  I asked because the type of error you are encountering is one we ran into when we first launched RRPP 1.0 and was fixed in either version 1.1.0 or 1.1.1 (see news <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RRPP/news/news.html> here).  Version 1.4.0 is current.  This was in 2021, so I might not recall correctly.

It is not possible to chase ghosts with your dilemma.  The only recommendation I have at this point is to use the most up to date versions of geomorph and RRPP, via:

install.packages("devtools”)
devtools::install_github("mlcollyer/RRPP", build_vignettes = TRUE)
devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph", build_vignettes = TRUE)

Whether this will work with R 4.1.1 or the dependencies of these packages, which have also surely been updated the last two years, I cannot say.  CRAN provides archives of past packages so you might be able to install old versions of the packages that will work for you but lack any other updates that came after.  We simply cannot retroactively fix old packages to work with old versions of R, so you might need to upgrade your operating system and work with more current software.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear members of the list,

I am in correspondence with Aleksandar in regard to the problem outlined and I would like to point out a few things.

1. Calculation of mean shapes problem
Lisso.means <- lapply (coords.subset(gdf$shape, classifier$Species), FUN = mshape) will return a list. The list should be converted to an array of appropriate dimensionality before being used in the downstream analysis in the geomorph.

Lisso.means1 <-as.matrix (Lisso.means) will not make it an array but rather one solution is to use the following code:

Lisso.means.array <- array (unlist( Lisso.means ), dim = c( 13, 3 , length (Lisso.means)))

Caution should be about the order of mean shapes and the following can help:

dimnames(Lisso.means.array)[[3]] <-  unique (gsub (pattern = '[0-9]+', replacement = "", names (unlist( Lisso.means ))))

2.  Aleksandar uses a tree without information about branch lengths. This is a typical approach when published phylogenies do not contain all the taxa researchers have in the shape data and they are forced to combine phylogenetic information (just topologies) from several different papers.
It seems that the geomorph requires phylogeny WITH branch lengths (e.g. tree$edge.length != NULL)  and therefore all phylogenetic analyses are not applicable to situations where just simple tree topology is provided like in Aleksandars' case (e.g. many scientists draw just tree topology in Mesquite or generate such trees in R). Let's see an example:

library (geomorph)
library (ape)

## currently geomorph does handle ONLY phylogenies with branch lengths
data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy)
summary(PCA.w.phylo)
plot(PCA.w.phylo, phylo = TRUE, main = "PCA.w.phylo")

is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengts

## let's try to work around with a tree without branch lengths (just tree topology)
plethspecies$phy$edge.length <- NULL
is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) #  TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths

PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy) # this will not work and the error will appear "Error in edge[, 3] : subscript out of bounds"

This is because gm.prcomp function calls anc.BM function and anc.BM further calls reorder.phy internally. reorder.phy assumes that phy has edge.lengths as the second line of the code in the function is 'edge.length <- phy$edge.length'. If phy$edge.length == NULL (like in the case of a tree with just topology information) the function will return the error outlined.

Possible solution:
# generate just tree topology in R (one can use other software as well...)
treeWithFixedBranches <- ape::read.tree(text = "(Species 1, (Species 2, (Species 3, (Species 4, (Species 5, Species 6)))));")
is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length)  # TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths

# plot the tree
plot (treeWithFixedBranches)

# find the order of branches in the tree
edgelabels()

# manually construct the branch lengths in order that appear in the tree
brLengths <- c (1, 0.2, 4*0.2, 0.2, 3*0.2, 0.2, 2*0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)

# add the branch length information to the tree
treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length <- brLengths

# plot the same tree with fixed branch lengths
plot (treeWithFixedBranches) # it has the same topology as the tree with just topology information
is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengths

___________

The geomorph will handle such manually added branch lengths to a tree that is constructed with just topology information. The little trick can expand the usage of geomorph to researchers who are interested (just) in tree topology. I suggest that reorder.phy can be extended in a way to return the message (alongside the error) if the tree provided does not have branch lengths (e.g. 'if (is.null (phy$edge.length)) stop ("The phylogenetic tree does not have branch lengths...")')

One should be clear about the justification of using a tree with just topology in the downstream analysis as the little trick will solve the problem "just technically" in order to be able to apply the geomorph functions related to comparative methods.

Kind regards,
Marko

> Dear members of the list,

> I am in correspondence with Aleksandar in regard to the problem outlined and I would like to point out a few things.
>
> 1. Calculation of mean shapes problem
> Lisso.means <- lapply (coords.subset(gdf$shape, classifier$Species), FUN = mshape) will return a list. The list should be converted to an array of appropriate dimensionality before being used in the downstream analysis in the geomorph.
>
> Lisso.means1 <-as.matrix (Lisso.means) will not make it an array but rather one solution is to use the following code:
> Lisso.means.array <- array (unlist( Lisso.means ), dim = c( 13, 3 , length (Lisso.means)))
>
> Caution should be about the order of mean shapes and the following can help:
>
> dimnames(Lisso.means.array)[[3]] <-  unique (gsub (pattern = '[0-9]+', replacement = "", names (unlist( Lisso.means ))))
>
> 2.  Aleksandar uses a tree without information about branch lengths. This is a typical approach when published phylogenies do not contain all the taxa researchers have in the shape data and they are forced to combine phylogenetic information (just topologies) from several different papers.
> It seems that the geomorph requires phylogeny WITH branch lengths (e.g. tree$edge.length != NULL)  and therefore all phylogenetic analyses are not applicable to situations where just simple tree topology is provided like in Aleksandars' case (e.g. many scientists draw just tree topology in Mesquite or generate such trees in R). Let's see an example:
>
> library (geomorph)
> library (ape)
>
> ## currently geomorph does handle ONLY phylogenies with branch lengths
> data(plethspecies)
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
> PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy)
> summary(PCA.w.phylo)
> plot(PCA.w.phylo, phylo = TRUE, main = "PCA.w.phylo")
>
> is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengts
>
> ## let's try to work around with a tree without branch lengths (just tree topology)
> plethspecies$phy$edge.length <- NULL
> is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) #  TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths
>
> PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy) # this will not work and the error will appear "Error in edge[, 3] : subscript out of bounds"
>
> This is because gm.prcomp function calls anc.BM function and anc.BM further calls reorder.phy internally. reorder.phy assumes that phy has edge.lengths as the second line of the code in the function is 'edge.length <- phy$edge.length'. If phy$edge.length == NULL (like in the case of a tree with just topology information) the function will return the error outlined.
>
> Possible solution:
> # generate just tree topology in R (one can use other software as well...)
> treeWithFixedBranches <- ape::read.tree(text = "(Species 1, (Species 2, (Species 3, (Species 4, (Species 5, Species 6)))));")
> is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length)  # TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths
>
> # plot the tree
> plot (treeWithFixedBranches)
>
> # find the order of branches in the tree
> edgelabels()
>
> # manually construct the branch lengths in order that appear in the tree
> brLengths <- c (1, 0.2, 4*0.2, 0.2, 3*0.2, 0.2, 2*0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)
>
> # add the branch length information to the tree
> treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length <- brLengths
>
> # plot the same tree with fixed branch lengths
> plot (treeWithFixedBranches) # it has the same topology as the tree with just topology information
> is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengths
>
> ___________
>
> The geomorph will handle such manually added branch lengths to a tree that is constructed with just topology information. The little trick can expand the usage of geomorph to researchers who are interested (just) in tree topology. I suggest that reorder.phy can be extended in a way to return the message (alongside the error) if the tree provided does not have branch lengths (e.g. 'if (is.null (phy$edge.length)) stop ("The phylogenetic tree does not have branch lengths...")')
>
> One should be clear about the justification of using a tree with just topology in the downstream analysis as the little trick will solve the problem "just technically" in order to be able to apply the geomorph functions related to comparative methods.
>
> Kind regards,
> Marko

Dear Marko,

Thanks for the suggestions.  With respect to the responses below, any opinions are my own and I do not wish for them to represent the geomorph team.

> On Nov 3, 2023, at 10:01 AM, Marko Djurakic <zmijo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear members of the list,
>
> I am in correspondence with Aleksandar in regard to the problem outlined and I would like to point out a few things.
>
> 1. Calculation of mean shapes problem
> Lisso.means <- lapply (coords.subset(gdf$shape, classifier$Species), FUN = mshape) will return a list. The list should be converted to an array of appropriate dimensionality before being used in the downstream analysis in the geomorph.

Yes, lapply means list-apply.  This is a base R function and should return a list.

>
> Lisso.means1 <-as.matrix (Lisso.means) will not make it an array but rather one solution is to use the following code:
> Lisso.means.array <- array (unlist( Lisso.means ), dim = c( 13, 3 , length (Lisso.means)))
>
> Caution should be about the order of mean shapes and the following can help:
>
> dimnames(Lisso.means.array)[[3]] <-  unique (gsub (pattern = '[0-9]+', replacement = "", names (unlist( Lisso.means ))))

This seems like a lot of work.  Why not use simplify2array?  here is an example:

> n <- 20

>
> 2.  Aleksandar uses a tree without information about branch lengths. This is a typical approach when published phylogenies do not contain all the taxa researchers have in the shape data and they are forced to combine phylogenetic information (just topologies) from several different papers.
> It seems that the geomorph requires phylogeny WITH branch lengths (e.g. tree$edge.length != NULL)  and therefore all phylogenetic analyses are not applicable to situations where just simple tree topology is provided like in Aleksandars' case (e.g. many scientists draw just tree topology in Mesquite or generate such trees in R). Let's see an example:
>
> library (geomorph)
> library (ape)
>
> ## currently geomorph does handle ONLY phylogenies with branch lengths
> data(plethspecies)
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
> PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy)
> summary(PCA.w.phylo)
> plot(PCA.w.phylo, phylo = TRUE, main = "PCA.w.phylo")
>
> is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengts
>
> ## let's try to work around with a tree without branch lengths (just tree topology)
> plethspecies$phy$edge.length <- NULL
> is.null(plethspecies$phy$edge.length) #  TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths
>
> PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy) # this will not work and the error will appear "Error in edge[, 3] : subscript out of bounds"
>
> This is because gm.prcomp function calls anc.BM function and anc.BM further calls reorder.phy internally. reorder.phy assumes that phy has edge.lengths as the second line of the code in the function is 'edge.length <- phy$edge.length'. If phy$edge.length == NULL (like in the case of a tree with just topology information) the function will return the error outlined.
>
> Possible solution:
> # generate just tree topology in R (one can use other software as well...)
> treeWithFixedBranches <- ape::read.tree(text = "(Species 1, (Species 2, (Species 3, (Species 4, (Species 5, Species 6)))));")
> is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length)  # TRUE, the tree does not have branch lengths
>
> # plot the tree
> plot (treeWithFixedBranches)
>
> # find the order of branches in the tree
> edgelabels()
>
> # manually construct the branch lengths in order that appear in the tree
> brLengths <- c (1, 0.2, 4*0.2, 0.2, 3*0.2, 0.2, 2*0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)
>
> # add the branch length information to the tree
> treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length <- brLengths
>
> # plot the same tree with fixed branch lengths
> plot (treeWithFixedBranches) # it has the same topology as the tree with just topology information
> is.null (treeWithFixedBranches$edge.length) # FALSE, the tree has branch lengths
>

The ape::compute.brlen can add branch lengths rather easily, and can accommodate different methods for estimating branch lengths, but in order to calculate phylogenetic signal, branch lengths are required.  (We could probably add a trap to catch this and stop the analysis.)  The problem will be in estimation of the covariance matrix — there are no covariances if there are no descriptions of shared evolutionary history based on branch lengths).  demo below.

> attributes(tree)
$names
[1] "edge"      "tip.label" "Nnode"

$class
[1] "phylo"

$order
[1] "cladewise"

> tree2 <- compute.brlen(tree)
> attributes(tree2)
$names
[1] "edge"        "tip.label"   "Nnode"       "edge.length"

$class
[1] "phylo"

$order
[1] "cladewise"

> ___________
>
> The geomorph will handle such manually added branch lengths to a tree that is constructed with just topology information. The little trick can expand the usage of geomorph to researchers who are interested (just) in tree topology. I suggest that reorder.phy can be extended in a way to return the message (alongside the error) if the tree provided does not have branch lengths (e.g. 'if (is.null (phy$edge.length)) stop ("The phylogenetic tree does not have branch lengths...")')

You call this a little trick.  I would call it forced dogma.  If we add support functions that calculate branch lengths we impose whatever method we use as the rule.  I would rather not do that.  It influences estimation of the phylogenetic covariance matrix.   If the tree has branch lengths already, the user can scale these based on some notion of what the internal branch scaling parameter, lambda, should be and the rescaled tree can be used.  Some prior manipulation has to be up to the user and not the function, in my opinion.

>
> One should be clear about the justification of using a tree with just topology in the downstream analysis as the little trick will solve the problem "just technically" in order to be able to apply the geomorph functions related to comparative methods.

Again, I would not consider obtaining a result to be a solution if it asserts personal philosophy into how the result was obtained.  I appreciate learning that this was caused by using a tree with no branch lengths.  The error — indicating a lack of a numeric matrix — must have been triggered by a missing covariance matrix.  How this could elude the original calculation of the covariance matrix is an interesting problem, but one I think we already fixed versions ago.  I could be wrong — I will confirm.  However, forcing a tree to have branch lengths so that physignal would work would be software malpractice, in my opinion, because it provides results where results should not be provided until the researcher has asserted what the branch lengths should be.
>
> Kind regards,
> Marko

Likewise,
Mike

> You call this a little trick.  I would call it forced dogma.  If we add support functions that calculate branch lengths we impose whatever method we use as the rule.  I would rather not do that.  It influences estimation of the phylogenetic covariance matrix.   If the tree has branch lengths already, the user can scale these based on some notion of what the internal branch scaling parameter, lambda, should be and the rescaled tree can be used.  Some prior manipulation has to be up to the user and not the function, in my opinion.

I appreciate learning that this was caused by using a tree with no branch lengths.  The error — indicating a lack of a numeric matrix — must have been triggered by a missing covariance matrix.  How this could elude the original calculation of the covariance matrix is an interesting problem, but one I think we already fixed versions ago.  I could be wrong — I will confirm.  However, forcing a tree to have branch lengths so that physignal would work would be software malpractice, in my opinion, because it provides results where results should not be provided until the researcher has asserted what the branch lengths should be.

messages.subject: Updates based on previous thread
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

This is probably a mostly unneeded announcement of an update.  Based on the previous thread, I added traps to the code to return an error that states, “The tree has no branch lengths” rather than an unhelpful base R error.  If you would like to have this non-operational update in your current R libraries, the following code allows installation:

install.packages("devtools”)
devtools::install_github("mlcollyer/RRPP", build_vignettes = TRUE)
devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph", build_vignettes = TRUE)

In case anyone likes programming hints, I discovered one reason for the abstruse error was a function within a function; i.e.,

functionB <- function(x) trcrossprod(functionA(x))

If the error is caused by functionA, the error statement suggests it is functionB or the other function used, in this case, tcrossprod.  This is why no issue with branch lengths was returned.  The updated functions now check for branch lengths and stops analysis if there are none.

Best,
Mike

Hi All,

I am hoping to please ask a question here about the use of Checkpoint to undertake landmarking prior to analysis in geomorph.

I know it isn't explicitly related to geomorph, but I want to be certain I am doing my landmarking correctly prior to importing landmarks and trying to analyse them in geomorph.

In Stratovan Checkpoint I am currently placing landmarks on my specimens. I am using 3 separate templates for each specimen. This is split by (1) surface/patch landmark template, (2) curve landmarks template and (3) fixed single point landmark template.

Is this an appropriate approach to placing landmarks on each specimen? Can I use 3 separate templates per specimen and then export the entire landmark data set (3 types of landmarks) from checkpoint into geomorph for analysis? Or is there any known issues with using multiple templates on specimens?

Any advice and tips about using Checkpoint prior to 3DGM analysis would be greatly appreciated. I want to avoid any issues with landmarking & my data sets prior to analysis where possible.

Thanks,
Kate :)

 From what I understand, the coefficients used to measure modularity/integration do so at the sample level. I'm wondering if there is a way of measuring these in a structure at the individual level (i.e., as in fluctuating asymmetry where sample and individual measures can be computed) to explore patterns of within-group variation?

 Any reference to past research or thoughts on feasibility would be greatly appreciated!

The short answer is no. Integration and modularity are measured at the sample level because they are defined in terms of the degree of covariation within modules versus between modules. One cannot have covariation without at least two observations/specimens.
